slides.title: What are quantum dots?
points: Quantum dots are semiconductor nanocrystals so small that charge carriers are confined in all three dimensions, giving size-dependent optical and electronic properties.
slides.say: Use TV color dots or bio-imaging particles as familiar examples.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Why quantum dots behave differently
points: Their diameter is comparable to exciton Bohr radius.
Electrons and holes cannot move as freely as in bulk.
Many atoms lie at or near the surface, so surface chemistry matters.
slides.say: Stress that quantum dots are not just small particles; size changes physics.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Quantum confinement effect
points: Quantum confinement occurs when a particle is small enough that electron and hole motion is restricted, causing energy levels and band gap to depend on size.
slides.say: Explain smaller dots usually require more energy and emit shorter wavelength light.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Size controls color
slides.say: Ask students which dot emits higher-energy light.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Surface-to-volume ratio increases sharply
points: As particle size decreases, the fraction of atoms at the surface increases, making surface chemistry strongly influence reactivity, stability and optical behavior.
slides.say: Explain why capping agents are important in quantum dot synthesis.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Band gap is size dependent
slides.say: Connect band gap to color and solar-energy absorption.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Quantum dot properties
points: Strong absorption and efficient emission are possible.
Surface ligands control stability and compatibility.
Useful in LEDs, sensors, imaging and solar cells.
slides.say: Keep properties tied to applications.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Cd-Se quantum dots
points: Cadmium selenide quantum dots are II-VI semiconductor nanocrystals widely used to demonstrate size-tunable optical properties.
slides.say: Mention toxicity awareness briefly but keep scope to syllabus.

slides.title: Wet chemical synthesis idea
points: Wet chemical synthesis forms quantum dots by reacting precursor chemicals in solution under controlled nucleation and growth conditions.
slides.say: Explain it is solution-based chemistry.

slides.title: Controlling Cd-Se quantum dot size
points: Higher temperature can speed nucleation and growth.
Longer growth generally increases particle size.
Stabilizes surface and limits uncontrolled growth.
slides.say: Connect each variable to final optical property.

slides.title: Cd-Se synthesis memory trick

slides.title: Applications of quantum dots
points: Quantum-dot color conversion for high color purity.

Optical response changes with environment or analyte.
Bright nanoscale labels, with toxicity/biocompatibility care.

slides.title: What is a QDSSC?
points: A quantum dot sensitized solar cell uses quantum dots as light absorbers attached to a wide band-gap semiconductor such as TiO2 to generate electrical energy.

slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: QDSSC construction
points: Transparent conducting glass coated with TiO2 and quantum dots.
Absorb light and inject electrons into TiO2.
Completes electron transfer in the external circuit.

slides.title: Why quantum dots help solar cells
points: Can tune absorption by dot size.
Different QDs cover different spectral regions.
Solution methods can support low-cost fabrication routes.

slides.title: What is a polymer?
points: A polymer is a high-molecular-weight macromolecule formed by repeated linking of small units called monomers.
slides.say: Use nylon, PVC and PMMA as examples that appear later.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Why polymer molecular weight matters
points: Usually improve strength, toughness and viscosity.
Real polymer samples contain many chain lengths.
Molecular weight affects melting, flow and shaping.
Mechanical, thermal and chemical behavior depend on chain size.
slides.say: Set up Mn and Mw.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Number-average molecular weight

definition.text: Mn = Σ Ni Mi / Σ Ni Ni = number of molecules of molar mass Mi Counts every molecule equally

points: Use the formula as a marks anchor: define symbols, substitute carefully, show units where needed, and interpret the result.
slides.say: Explain Mn is sensitive to the number of molecules in each fraction.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Weight-average molecular weight

definition.text: Mw = Σ Ni Mi² / Σ Ni Mi Large molecules contribute more strongly because mass weighting is used

points: Use the formula as a marks anchor: define symbols, substitute carefully, show units where needed, and interpret the result.
slides.say: Explain Mw emphasizes heavier chains more than Mn.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Mn vs Mw comparison
points: Lower than or equal to Mw
Indicates property impact of large chains
slides.say: Mention Mw is usually greater than Mn for a distribution.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Polydispersity index
points: Polydispersity index is Mw/Mn; it indicates how broad the polymer molecular-weight distribution is.
slides.say: Even if not in title, PDI is natural after Mn and Mw.

slides.say: Show that polymer behavior is designed, not accidental.

slides.title: Crystallinity improves order
points: Crystallinity is the degree of ordered packing in polymer chains; higher crystallinity generally increases density, strength and chemical resistance.
slides.say: Contrast amorphous and crystalline regions.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Strength depends on chain interactions
points: Longer chains can entangle and resist pulling.
Hydrogen bonding and polarity improve attraction.
Ordered regions can reinforce the material.
Network structure can increase rigidity and thermal stability.
slides.say: Use nylon as strong because of hydrogen bonding.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Elasticity depends on chain mobility
points: Can uncoil and recoil under stress.
More amorphous freedom can increase flexibility.
Moderate crosslinks help recovery; too many make brittle material.
Above glass transition, chains move more easily.
slides.say: Relate to rubber-like materials without leaving syllabus too far.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Chemical resistivity depends on structure
points: Controls interaction with solvents and chemicals.
Tight packing reduces penetration of chemicals.
Chlorine, ester or amide groups change resistance.

slides.title: Nylon-6,6 is a condensation polymer
points: Nylon-6,6 is a polyamide formed by condensation polymerization of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, with amide linkages in the chain.
slides.say: Explain 6,6 comes from six carbon atoms in each monomer.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Properties of nylon-6,6
points: Chain packing and hydrogen bonding improve mechanical strength.
Useful in fibers and engineering parts.
Amide groups can interact with water.
slides.say: Connect amide linkages with hydrogen bonding.
slides.ask: Ask students to connect structure, size or molecular weight with the final material property.

slides.title: Nylon-6,6 in 3D printing applications
points: Useful where printed parts need impact resistance.
Good for gears, fixtures and moving components.
Better mechanical performance than many simple plastics.
3D printing can form complex nylon components.
slides.say: Mention drying nylon before printing as a practical note.

slides.title: What is a conducting polymer?
points: A conducting polymer is an organic polymer with a conjugated backbone that can conduct electricity, especially after doping.
slides.say: Explain ordinary polymers are usually insulators, but conjugated polymers are different.
